title: Some, any, none
goal: Say what you eat and drink with du, de la, de l' and des, and what you don't with pas de.

blocks.title: Breakfast in Montréal
blocks.context: Camille and her new roommate Nguyen talk about breakfast.

lines.speaker: Nguyen
lines.fr: Bonjour Camille ! Qu'est-ce que tu manges le matin ?
lines.en: Morning, Camille! What do you eat in the morning?

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Je mange du pain avec du fromage, et je bois du café. Et toi ?
lines.en: I eat bread with cheese, and I drink coffee. And you?

lines.speaker: Nguyen
lines.fr: Moi, je ne mange pas de pain le matin. Je mange du riz ou des fruits.
lines.en: I don't eat bread in the morning. I eat rice or fruit.

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Du riz le matin ? C'est intéressant ! Tu bois du café ?
lines.en: Rice in the morning? That's interesting! Do you drink coffee?

lines.speaker: Nguyen
lines.fr: Non, je ne bois pas de café. Je bois du thé.
lines.en: No, I don't drink coffee. I drink tea.

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Moi, j'aime le café, et toi, tu aimes le thé. C'est parfait !
lines.en: I like coffee, and you like tea. That's perfect!

blocks.title: Karim's lunch
blocks.context: Karim talks about what he eats at lunchtime.
blocks.fr: Le midi, je mange de la viande ou du poisson avec des légumes. Je bois de l'eau. Je ne mange pas de pâtes, et je ne bois pas de jus d'orange.
blocks.en: At lunchtime, I eat meat or fish with vegetables. I drink water. I don't eat pasta, and I don't drink orange juice.

blocks.body: Look at the little words before the food: [[du]], [[de la]], [[de l']], [[des]]… and just [[de]] after [[ne… pas]]. That is today's lesson.

steps.title: Du, de la, de l', des

blocks.title: Why French needs “some”
blocks.body:
In English, you can say “I eat bread” with no article. **French can't.** A food noun almost always needs a little word in front of it.

When you eat or drink **an amount** of something (not all bread in the world, not one specific loaf, just *some*), French uses the **partitive**: [[du]], [[de la]], [[de l']] or [[des]].

[[Je mange du pain.]] = I eat (some) bread. In English, “some” is optional; in French, [[du]] is required.

blocks.title: The partitive
head: before the noun
example
English
blocks.note: [[de + le]] always contracts to [[du]]. [[de la]] and [[de l']] never contract.

blocks.title: Eating and drinking
blocks.pattern: je mange / je bois + du / de la / de l' / des + food
blocks.note: Use the partitive after verbs like [[manger]] (to eat), [[boire]] (to drink) and [[acheter]] (to buy), when you mean an amount. (Exception: [[ce n'est pas du café]] keeps [[du]]; see below.)

examples.en: Are you eating pasta? (to a friend)

blocks.title: Boire (to drink): three forms to know now
head: boire
English
rows: you drink (formal, or more than one person)
blocks.note: [[boire]] is irregular. Learn these as chunks for now. You will also hear [[il boit]] / [[elle boit]] (sounds the same as [[bois]]) and [[nous buvons]].

blocks.title: None: pas de
blocks.body:
After a negative (**ne … pas**), [[du]], [[de la]], [[de l']] and [[des]] all become just [[de]]. Before a vowel, [[de]] becomes [[d']].

- [[Je mange du pain.]] → [[Je ne mange pas de pain.]]
- [[Je mange de la viande.]] → [[Je ne mange pas de viande.]]
- [[Je bois de l'eau.]] → [[Je ne bois pas d'eau.]]
- [[Je mange des fruits.]] → [[Je ne mange pas de fruits.]]

It works the same way with [[avoir]]: [[J'ai des enfants]] → [[Je n'ai pas d'enfants]].

**Exception: être.** After [[ce n'est pas]], the article does **not** change: [[C'est du café ? Non, ce n'est pas du café, c'est du thé.]]

blocks.title: Liking vs eating: le or du?
blocks.body:
This is the key contrast of the unit:

- **Liking** (aimer, adorer, détester) → [[le]], [[la]], [[l']], [[les]]: you talk about the food **in general**. [[J'aime le café.]]
- **Eating, drinking, buying** (manger, boire, acheter) → [[du]], [[de la]], [[de l']], [[des]]: you talk about **an amount**. [[Je bois du café.]]

And in the negative, only the partitive changes: [[Je n'aime pas le café]] (the article stays), but [[Je ne bois pas de café]].

- [[Je mange le pain]] is not wrong, but it means *the* bread (a specific one, on the table). For “I eat bread”, say [[Je mange du pain]].
- [[J'aime du café]] is wrong. After aimer, use [[le]]: [[J'aime le café]].
- [[Je ne mange pas du pain]] is wrong. After ne… pas, use [[de]]: [[Je ne mange pas de pain]].
- [[Je ne bois pas de l'eau]] is wrong. Say [[Je ne bois pas d'eau]].
- [[Je n'aime pas de fromage]] is wrong. With aimer, the article stays: [[Je n'aime pas le fromage]].
- But [[Ce n'est pas de café]] is wrong: with être, keep the article: [[Ce n'est pas du café.]]

blocks.title: Why des looks familiar
blocks.body:
You already know [[des]] as the plural of [[un]] / [[une]]: [[un enfant]] → [[des enfants]]. With food, [[des]] works the same way: it means “some” of something plural, so you don't need to choose between two meanings.

For foods you count (apples, vegetables), use [[une pomme]] / [[des pommes]]. For foods you don't count (bread, water, rice), use [[du]], [[de la]], [[de l']].

blocks.title: Drinks in Canada
blocks.body:
- In Québec, people often call a soft drink [[une liqueur]] (informal). The standard word, used on menus and labels, is [[une boisson gazeuse]]. Careful: in France, [[une liqueur]] is a sweet **alcoholic** drink, and a soft drink is [[un soda]].
- On milk cartons in Canada, you will see [[lait 1 %]], [[lait 2 %]] (said *deux pour cent*) and [[lait 3,25 %]] for whole milk.
- [[Je bois du lait 2 %.]] is a perfectly normal Canadian sentence!

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: [[du]] has the French *u* sound (lips round, tongue forward). [[des]] sounds like “day”. [[de]] is a short, soft “duh”.

lines.tip: du: round your lips as for “oo”, but say “ee”.
des = “day”; the s of fruits is silent.

blocks.prompt: A new colleague asks about your habits. Say what you eat and drink in the morning and at lunch, and one thing you never eat or drink.
checklist: Le matin, je mange… / je bois…
Je ne mange pas de… / Je ne bois pas de…
Correct du / de la / de l' / des

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Le matin, je mange du pain et des fruits, et je bois du café. Le midi, je mange du poulet avec du riz. Je ne bois pas de lait.
models.en: In the morning, I eat bread and fruit, and I drink coffee. At lunch, I eat chicken with rice. I don't drink milk.

blocks.prompt: Write a note to your new roommate about food: what you eat and drink in the morning, what you like, and what you don't eat.
checklist: Use je mange / je bois + du, de la, de l' or des
Use j'aime + le, la, l' or les
End with a question for your roommate

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Salut ! Le matin, je mange des fruits et du pain, et je bois du thé. J'aime beaucoup le fromage. Je ne mange pas de viande et je ne bois pas de café. Et toi, tu bois du café ?
models.en: Hi! In the morning, I eat fruit and bread, and I drink tea. I really like cheese. I don't eat meat and I don't drink coffee. And you, do you drink coffee?

summary:
- Use [[du, de la, de l', des]] for an amount: [[Je mange du pain. Je bois de l'eau.]]
- After ne… pas, use [[de]] / [[d']]: [[Je ne mange pas de viande.]]
- Keep [[le / la / les]] with aimer: [[J'aime le café]], but [[je bois du café]]
- Say [[je bois, tu bois, vous buvez]]
